title: Miharban's telling
hook: a janamsakhi from the line of Prithi Chand, more reflective, full of discourse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bala: warm tellings framed as a friend's memories, with historians still asking whether he was there. Your line was told by a friend.

Families have them: the uncle who fell out with everyone over the will, years ago. Nobody quite forgives him. And yet, when the old photos come out, he's the one who remembers the names, the places, what grandfather used to say at the table. You'd rather not need him. But he kept the old papers, and he's thought hard about them. Sikh history has a telling of Guru Nanak's life that comes from a line like that. Today: Miharban's telling.
screen: `THE UNCLE WHO FELL OUT WITH EVERYONE.` → `HE STILL REMEMBERS THE NAMES.` → `A TELLING FROM A RIVAL LINE.`

segments.voice: Start with the family. Prithi Chand was the elder brother of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru. When Guru Ram Das chose Arjan as the next Guru, Prithi Chand did not accept it, and his line set itself up apart. Sikh tradition remembers them as rivals to the Gurus. Miharban was Prithi Chand's son, and a janamsakhi comes down under his name. It doesn't read like the plain Puratan stories or the warm, wonder-filled Bala ones. It's reflective. A sakhi sets the scene, and then the telling stops to talk: a discourse, a gosht, in which Guru Nanak's own hymns are explained in the setting of the story. It reads less like a storyteller and more like a teacher thinking aloud. So how do Sikhs read a book from that line? Carefully, and not all in the same way. Some keep their distance from it because of where it came from. Some historians and readers take it seriously as one more early witness, and value its long reflections on Nanak's hymns. Neither group pretends the family quarrel didn't happen. Here's the lesson in it. A telling from someone you'd rather not agree with can still add something: a detail, a reading, a question. Taking it in isn't the same as taking their side. And every telling adds something of its teller too, which is exactly why it's worth knowing who the teller was.
screen: `PRITHI CHAND, GURU ARJAN'S ELDER BROTHER.` · `MIHARBAN, HIS SON, AND HIS TELLING.` · `A SAKHI, THEN A DISCOURSE.` · `READ CAREFULLY, AND DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `EVERY TELLING ADDS.`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind, not someone dangerous, just someone whose views or choices you'd rather not share: a relative, a coworker, a voice you usually scroll past. Ask yourself one honest question, what might they know or notice that I don't, and let one possibility come; you don't have to agree with it, only hear it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.
